title: For its own sake (Avot 6:1)
hookLine: whoever learns for its own sake gains much and is called a friend
tomorrow: what do you owe someone who taught you one tiny thing?

cards: The email starts with thank you for your interest, and everyone knows how the next sentence goes. After a no like that, a real question shows up. If the answer is no, why keep doing the thing at all?
Avot's sixth chapter opens with an answer in one Hebrew word: lishmah. For its own sake.

teach.b: Rabbi Meir says: whoever studies Torah lishmah, for its own sake, gains many things, and the whole world is worth it for that person. They're called a friend, beloved, one who loves God and loves all creatures.
Here's the question under it: what does for its own sake mean, if the mishnah then lists rewards?

teach.h: WHAT COMES WHEN YOU STOP CHASING.
teach.b: The answer seems to be that these are things that come only when you stop chasing them. Study for the grade and you get a grade.
Study for the thing itself and you may end up a friend of God and of people, which no one can hand you.
The Talmud adds a kindness: start anyway, even for the wrong reasons, because from not for its own sake comes for its own sake. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: THE GITA: THE ACTION, NOT THE FRUIT.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the action alone, never to its fruits; don't let the fruit be your motive.
Two traditions, one shared insight: the work done for itself, without clutching at what it earns. And an honest difference.

The Gita speaks of action and duty on a battlefield, and asks to let go of the fruit entirely. Avot speaks of learning Torah, and still names what comes: a friend, beloved, a lover of God and of all creatures.
Each says it in its own words.

how: The ideal of Torah lishmah, learning for its own sake, runs through Jewish study; chapter six of Avot, which opens with Rabbi Meir's saying, is read on the last summer Shabbat afternoons of the Avot cycle.

o: learning a thing for itself, not a prize
studying in the name of your teacher
a vow to study in someone's memory

games.q: for its own sake — tap the pairs.

s: lishmah means expecting nothing good to come of it
Rabbi Meir lists what comes: a friend, beloved, one who loves God and all creatures.
the Bhagavad Gita also teaches acting without clinging to the fruit
Krishna tells Arjuna his right is to the action, never to its fruits.

games.q: you start volunteering at a food bank mostly to fill a résumé. a friend says that ruins it. what does the Talmud say?
o: start anyway: from not for its own sake comes for its own sake.
your friend is right: if it isn't lishmah, it doesn't count.
hide the real motive, and then it turns into lishmah.
games.why: the Talmud says to keep at Torah and good deeds even not for their own sake, because that path can lead to lishmah.

practice: Listen to one sound around you: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Don't use it for anything; don't name it, don't try to relax with it. Just listen to it for its own sake, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Lishmah: for its own sake. Rabbi Meir's word for learning done for itself, which turns out to be when the most comes.

carryVoice: Keep this close: for its own sake, and let the rest come to you unchased. Until tomorrow.
